title: List of Union quarantine pests and plant health import requirements
summary: Give feedback until 29 December 2026 on the EU’s updated list of Union quarantine pests and proposed …
update:
The European Commission is proposing changes to the European Union (EU) rules on plant health and on importing plants and plant products. The main changes for agri-food products are as follows.

Five new pests will be added to the EU quarantine pest list. These include tobacco budworm ( Chloridea virescens ) and yellow-striped armyworm ( Spodoptera ornithogalli and Spodoptera praefica ) affecting a wide range of crops, and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 (TR4) affecting bananas. Products containing these pests will not be allowed to enter the EU. No new specific import requirements are proposed for fresh fruit and vegetables. Three pests will be removed from the quarantine list. These are the citrus spiny whitefly, raspberry leaf curl virus, and strawberry leaf curl virus. There is currently not enough reliable scientific information to enable these pests to be identified and tested. New traceability requirements will apply in relation to false codling moth ( Thaumatotibia leucotreta, FCM). These requirements will apply to some fresh fruits (peppers, peaches, nectarines, pomegranates, certain citrus fruits) and to cut roses originating in Africa. Where these products are exported in packages, in addition to the phytosanitary certificate that is already required, exporters will have to include the codes identifying production places or sites on each package .

Competent authorities of countries that are members of the World Trade Organization can comment on this proposal until 29 December 2026 .
impacted_products: Peppers (Capsicum spp.), peaches, nectarines, pomegranates, citrus fruits (excluding lemons and limes), sweet oranges, grapevines, cut roses
what_changing:
The EU has notified the World Trade Organization Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (WTO SPS) Committee of a new draft proposal updating the EU list of Union quarantine pests and plant health import requirements ( G/SPS/N/EU/987 ). The proposal includes amendments to Regulation 2019/2072 , which establishes the EU’s phytosanitary requirements for plants and plant products.

why: The EU regularly reviews its plant health rules to prevent harmful pests from entering and spreading in its territory. Scientific risk assessments, notably by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), and pest risk analyses developed by the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO), inform these decisions. The European Commission, together with the EU Member States, decide which pests are listed as Union quarantine pests in Regulation 2019/2072 and adjusts the import requirements accordingly, taking into account interceptions at EU borders.
timeline:
The proposed Regulation is expected to be published in the first quarter of 2027.

The new package labelling requirements relating to FCM will apply 3 months after publication.

The revised list of quarantine pests will apply 6 months after publication.
actions: Competent authorities of countries that are members of the WTO can submit comments on the EU’s proposal by emailing the EU SPS Enquiry Point until 29 December 2026 ( G/SPS/N/EU/987 ).
background:
The EU has specific phytosanitary rules to prevent the introduction of FCM ( Thaumatotibia leucotreta ) into the EU (Regulation 2019/2072 , Annex VII, 62). These requirements apply to peppers ( Capsicum spp.), peaches and nectarines ( Prunus persica ), pomegranates ( Punica granatum ), certain citrus fruits, and cut roses ( Rosa spp.) originating from countries of the African continent, the islands of Cabo Verde, Madagascar, Mauritius, Réunion, and Saint Helena, and Israel. Sweet oranges ( Citrus sinensis ) are subject to separate requirements, including cold treatment (Annex VII, 62.1).

Exporters must comply with one of several phytosanitary options, including production in pest free places or sites of production, or the application of an approved systems approach or post-harvest treatment.

For further information see Exporting fresh Capsicum to the EU , which includes measures against FCM, using fresh peppers as an example.
